h1: Beer drinker personas: who your brewery is really for
title: Beer drinker personas for breweries | Craft Beer School
desc: Build up to three beer drinker personas from people you serve, write what matters for each and map how your brewery fits into their week.
teaser: Three well drawn drinkers will guide your rebrand better than a slide that says "25 to 40, urban, aspirational".
standfirst: A persona is a short portrait of a real kind of drinker, built from people who already come through your door. This guide shows how to write up to three, what to record for each and how to test them against your week, your menu and your positioning.
sections: A persona is someone you can picture at the bar

Describe your drinkers as people, not segments. Stop at three. Three is the right ceiling. One is too narrow for most taprooms. Five turns into a crowd nobody remembers by the next meeting.

A persona has a name, a job, a neighbourhood and habits. It should be specific enough that your head brewer, your floor manager and your designer picture the same person. If the description could fit half the city, it is a demographic, not a persona.
About ten conversations with regulars beat any survey

Do not invent your drinkers or borrow numbers from a survey you have not seen. Use what you have. Your floor staff know who orders the stout on a Tuesday. Your billing system shows which beers sell on which days. Your Instagram followers and WhatsApp group show who engages. Above all, talk to people.

Spend two weeks having short, friendly conversations with regulars. About ten interviews is enough. Ask what brought them in the first time, what else they drink, where they hear about new beer and who they come with. Write the answers down the same evening. Ask your billing system the same question in numbers: which beers sell before 7 pm on weekdays and which sell on Saturday afternoons. In a Hyderabad taproom those can be two different crowds with two different reasons to come. Patterns usually show by the eighth.
One page of 200 words per persona is enough

Record these fields for each one:

  • a first name and an age band, never below the legal drinking age in your state, which varies
  • work and neighbourhood, such as a nurse on rotating shifts in Gurugram
  • interests and the values they live by
  • the beer styles they order and the breweries they also visit
  • non-beer brands they trust, plus the food, music and books they like
  • how they find out about new beer

Add a photo, real or stock, so the team can see them. Keep each persona to one page of about 200 words.
A seven-day calendar shows where you fit

The question that matters most is how the brewery fits into each person's ordinary week. Answer it with a calendar. Lay out seven days and mark where your persona might meet you: a pint after a late shift, a Saturday lunch with family, a cricket screening with friends, a 500 ml can picked up for a house party.

In India many groups include people who do not drink. Plenty of outings are family ones too. If your persona brings a parent or a non-drinking friend, your food and alcohol-free options are part of the brand. Mark two or three real occasions per persona, not seven. A brewery that fits one evening a week well is doing its job.

Shortcuts like "the techie" or "the party crowd" feel efficient and mislead you. Build each persona from behaviour you have seen, not from assumptions about age, gender, region or religion. Women drink craft beer and should appear where you have met them, without gender becoming the whole personality. Drinkers in their 20s are not one group either. Our guide on younger drinkers and craft beer covers how their habits differ.

One more rule: no persona is defined by how much they drink. Build around occasions and taste, never volume.
Every persona should want what your position offers

Put the three personas next to your positioning matrix. Each should want what your position offers. If one keeps choosing a corner of the market you do not serve, you either drop that persona or change the position on purpose. Either is fine. Pretending is not.

The finished pages go to your designer as part of the strategy stage in our rebrand guide. Someone outside the brewery, used to writing for audiences in advertising, will notice when a persona is really the founder in disguise.

This week, book 60 minutes with two floor staff and draft three names with one line about each. The interviews fill in the rest.
Ankur Napa is a Master Brewer who also works in data and AI. Chatty Girija spent more than 30 years in advertising, hosts the Cheers Chatty Beer Podcast and teaches at Craft Beer School.
faqs: How many personas does a brewery need?
Up to three. More than that rarely stays in anyone's head long enough to guide a decision.
Can I use market research reports for personas?
Use only research you have read and can cite. The strongest personas come from your own regulars, floor staff and sales records.
Should personas include people who do not drink?
Your personas are drinkers of legal age, but note who they come with. Non-drinking friends and family shape the occasion, so food and alcohol-free options matter.
